blocks.text:
Design an elevator system for a building with multiple floors and multiple elevator cars. Riders press UP or DOWN on a floor, the system picks the best car to answer, and once inside they choose a destination. The system must serve everyone with low waiting time while never compromising safety.

Two design problems hide inside this everyday machine: each car is a state machine (idle, moving, doors open) that must behave safely in every state, and the controller is a scheduler that decides which car answers which call. The first is a State pattern problem; the second is a Strategy pattern problem, and keeping them separate is the whole design.

  • Actors: riders pressing buttons, the building system ticking the clock, and technicians taking cars in and out of service
  • Scope: one building, N floors, M cars, hall and cab calls, LOOK style scheduling, in memory simulation
  • Goal: a clean object oriented design where scheduling policy can change without touching the cars

An elevator is a state machine on rails, driven by a scheduler. Design the two separately and the problem falls apart into easy pieces.
These are the behaviours the system must support for riders and for the building. Every later decision traces back to this list.

metadata.alt: Functional requirements at a glance: calls, assignment, movement, doors, and safety

items: Hall calls: a rider on any floor presses UP or DOWN to request a pickup
Car assignment: the controller picks the best car for every hall call
Cab calls: a rider inside presses a destination floor button
Efficient movement: a car serves stops in sweep order, not in the order buttons were pressed
Doors: open on arrival, stay open a safe interval, reopen on obstruction
Status: every floor shows each car position and direction
Safety: overload detection blocks movement; emergency stop halts a car immediately
Maintenance: a car can be removed from and returned to service

blocks.text: An elevator carries people, so the quality bar is ordered: safety first, then service, then elegance.

metadata.alt: The five non-functional pillars, with safety on top

blocks.text: No scheduling decision may ever override a safety interlock. Doors closed before moving, no movement on overload, and emergency stop beats everything.
The scheduler exists to minimise how long riders wait and ride. The LOOK sweep and a sensible assignment strategy are the levers.
New scheduling policies, destination dispatch keypads, and VIP modes must plug in as new classes, because buildings retune elevators for their traffic all the time.
The same design must run 2 cars in a clinic or 12 cars in a tower. Nothing may hard code car counts or floor counts.
Buttons are pressed on many floors at the same instant. Request intake and stop assignment must be safe under concurrency, with duplicates collapsed.
Elevator scope varies wildly, so pin it down before designing. These questions separate a simulator from a control panel project.

items: Cars and floors: how many of each, and are there basements or restricted floors?
Scheduling: is nearest car acceptable, or do you want a smarter cost function?
Destination dispatch: classic two button halls, or type the floor before boarding?
Capacity: do we model weight and overload behaviour?
Simulation: is time a clock tick we control, or real threads?
Priorities: any VIP, freight, or fire service modes in scope?

blocks.text: Assumed answers for this design: M cars and N floors as constructor inputs; classic UP and DOWN hall buttons; nearest suitable car assignment behind a strategy interface; LOOK sweep per car; overload modelled; a step() clock tick drives the simulation; special modes discussed as extensions.
Saying these out loud keeps the interview scoped and honest.

items: Time: the world advances one step() at a time; one step moves a car one floor or toggles doors
Stops: each car keeps its pending stops in a sorted set, not a FIFO queue
Sweep rule: a car keeps its direction while any stop remains ahead, then reverses: the LOOK algorithm
Duplicates: pressing an already lit button is a no op
Assignment: a hall call is assigned to exactly one car at dispatch time
Safety: door and weight interlocks are modelled as guards the states must respect
State: in memory; the database section covers the persistent trip log

blocks.text: The nouns of the problem become the classes, each with one job.

metadata.alt: The core entities and how they connect

items: ElevatorController: the brain; receives every request and assigns it to a car through the strategy
Elevator: one car; knows its floor, direction, pending stops, and current state
ElevatorState: an interface with Idle, Moving, and DoorOpen implementations driving per tick behaviour
Request: an abstract call; HallRequest carries a direction, CabRequest carries just a floor
SchedulingStrategy: the pluggable policy that picks which car answers a hall call
Door: the car door with open, close, and obstruction handling
Display observers: floor panels that mirror car position and direction

blocks.text: Who owns whom is half the design conversation. All four relationship kinds appear here.

metadata.alt: Composition, association, and inheritance in the elevator system

items: Controller composes the car fleet: cars are created with the system and die with it
Each Elevator composes its Door: a door has no life apart from its car
Elevator aggregates its current state object: states are swapped as the car transitions
Controller aggregates observers: displays subscribe and unsubscribe freely
Controller uses the SchedulingStrategy: it calls pickCar and owns nothing inside the policy
States call back into their car: to move it, open doors, and read the stop set
HallRequest and CabRequest extend Request
IdleState, MovingState, DoorOpenState implement ElevatorState; NearestCarStrategy implements SchedulingStrategy

blocks.text: One picture holds the whole design: the controller drives the fleet through a strategy, and each car delegates its per tick behaviour to a state.

metadata.alt: UML class diagram of the elevator system

blocks.text: Reading guide: the filled diamond from controller to cars is composition, the open diamonds are aggregation, and the two dashed hierarchies, states and strategies, are the two patterns at the heart of the design.
Two patterns split the problem cleanly, and two more support them. Each earns its place with a reason.
Why needed: a car behaves differently per tick depending on whether it is idle, moving, or holding doors open. The same step() call must do three different things.

Why it is the best choice: the alternative is a status enum with a switch inside step(), which grows arms every time doors, safety, or new modes appear. One class per state keeps each behaviour small and testable.
What it solves: illegal actions like moving with open doors become impossible by construction, and adding a FireService or Maintenance state is one new class.

metadata.alt: The car states and their transitions

blocks.text: Why needed: which car answers a call is a business policy: nearest car, least loaded, zoned floors. Buildings tune this constantly.

Why it is the best choice: the policy is one pure decision, cars and request in, chosen car out, which is exactly a strategy interface. Hard coding it into the controller would force edits for every tuning.
What it solves: the controller stays frozen while policies compete; a new strategy is a new class and one constructor argument.
9.3 The LOOK sweep inside each car
blocks.content: 9.3 The LOOK sweep inside each car

blocks.text: Within a car, stop order is not a pattern but an algorithm: keep going in one direction while stops remain ahead, then reverse. It is the elevator version of the disk LOOK algorithm, and a sorted set makes it four lines of code.

metadata.alt: The LOOK sweep: serve everything ahead, then reverse

blocks.text: Displays are observers notified on every car move, keeping presentation out of the core. The controller is a facade: riders and the building talk to three methods and never touch cars directly.
State runs each car, Strategy picks between cars, LOOK orders the stops. Three ideas, one clean system.
blocks.content: State runs each car, Strategy picks between cars, LOOK orders the stops. Three ideas, one clean system.

blocks.text: Each class in one breath: responsibility, attributes, methods.

items: Responsibility: accept every request, deduplicate, assign to a car via the strategy, and tick the world
Attributes: cars, strategy, pending hall calls
Methods: requestPickup(floor, direction), requestFloor(carId, floor), step(), setMaintenance(carId), getStatus()
Responsibility: one car: hold position, direction, and stops; delegate each tick to its state
Attributes: id, currentFloor, direction, sorted stop set, state, door, capacity
Methods: addStop(floor), step(), nextStopInDirection(), reverse()
IdleState: if a stop exists, choose a direction and become Moving; otherwise rest
MovingState: advance one floor per tick; on reaching a stop, remove it and become DoorOpen
DoorOpenState: hold doors for the dwell time, reopen on obstruction, then close and return to Moving or Idle
HallRequest: floor plus desired direction, raised outside the car
CabRequest: a destination floor, raised inside a specific car
NearestCarStrategy: scores each car by distance and direction compatibility and returns the best
Responsibility: the safety boundary: open, close, and report obstruction
Methods: open(), close() returning false when blocked, isObstructed()

blocks.text: Two interfaces carry all the volatility: what a car does each tick, and how a car is chosen.

metadata.alt: The two interfaces and their implementations

blocks.text: Why ElevatorState is an interface: the car holds one reference and calls step() blindly; each mode decides what a tick means. Adding a mode never touches the car.
Why SchedulingStrategy is an interface: assignment is a pure function that buildings want to swap. Keeping it stateless makes strategies trivially testable: feed cars, assert the pick.
Three workflows tell the story: a simple pickup, two calls merged into one sweep, and safety overriding everything.

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of a hall call answered and a destination served

blocks.text: The button talks only to the controller, the strategy picks car 2, and from there the car handles everything: arrival, doors, and the cab call to floor 12.

metadata.alt: Two riders on the way up are served by one car in floor order

blocks.text: Riders at 3 and 7 both want to go up while the car climbs from 2. The sorted stop set serves them in floor order, 3 then 7, regardless of who pressed first. This is the LOOK sweep visible in a sequence.

metadata.alt: Overload keeps the doors open and the car parked until weight is normal

blocks.text: The weight sensor outranks the scheduler. The car refuses to move, keeps doors open, and resumes only when the load is safe. No state may ignore a safety guard.
The request pipeline is short, and every arrow has a reason.

metadata.alt: From button press to a served stop

items: A rider presses UP on floor 5; the controller receives requestPickup(5, UP)
Duplicate check: if floor 5 UP is already pending, the press is ignored
The strategy scores all in service cars and picks the best
addStop(5) inserts the floor into that car sorted stop set
The car sweeps to floor 5, opens doors, and the rider boards
The cab call 12 is added; the car continues the sweep and delivers
All cars in maintenance: the controller rejects with NoCarAvailable and the hall panel shows out of service
Door obstruction: DoorOpen state reopens and restarts the dwell timer; repeated obstruction raises an alert
Overload: the car parks with doors open until weight drops
Car pulled mid trip: its unserved stops are re dispatched to other cars through the same strategy
Invalid floor: rejected instantly with InvalidFloor, no state touched

blocks.text: Riders see two calls; the building sees three more. Everything else is internal.

blocks.text: Failures are explicit, specific, and never corrupt a car.

metadata.alt: The failure categories and their exceptions

items: InvalidFloorException: a floor outside the building, rejected before any dispatch
UnknownCarException: a cab call naming a car that does not exist
NoCarAvailableException: every car is out of service; the hall call is refused loudly, not queued silently
CarInMaintenanceException: direct requests to a pulled car are rejected
OverloadException: movement refused while weight exceeds capacity
DoorObstructedException: close attempts fail safely and reopen
Emergency stop: a Halted state that only a technician reset can leave
Guarantee: every exception leaves stop sets and states consistent; a failed dispatch assigns nothing

blocks.text: The contention point is the controller intake, not the cars. Many floors press buttons in the same instant.

metadata.alt: Concurrent identical calls collapse into one stop through the synchronized intake

items: Duplicate hall calls: two riders press floor 5 UP together; the system must create one stop, not two
Assign versus maintenance: a car being pulled exactly as the strategy picks it
Stop set mutation: a cab call added while the state is choosing the next stop

blocks.text: The rule mirrors every LLD problem: make the check and the change one atomic step, and lock the smallest thing. Intake and dedup lock the pending set; each car stop set is a concurrent sorted set; maintenance flips inside the same lock as assignment.
The pending set add is the same atomic check and act used on parking spots and vending shelves: exactly one of two identical presses proceeds, and the loser costs nothing.
Elevator systems are tuned for decades, so extension paths matter more than the first version.

metadata.alt: Extensions plug into the strategy, the states, and the observers

items: New scheduling policy: least loaded, zoned floors, or up peak morning mode: one new SchedulingStrategy
Destination dispatch: lobby keypads become HallRequests carrying a destination; the strategy gains better information, nothing else changes
VIP or freight mode: one new state that ignores hall calls while active
Energy saving: an idle parking strategy that spreads waiting cars across floors
Lobby displays and analytics: observers on car events, zero core changes

blocks.text: Future enhancements: fire service mode, earthquake parking, and group control across towers all arrive as states and strategies on the same skeleton.
The design earns each principle through its structure.

metadata.alt: How the elevator design maps to SOLID

items: Single Responsibility: cars move, states define per mode behaviour, the strategy assigns, the controller coordinates
Open Closed: policies, modes, and displays extend as new classes; the tick loop never changes
Liskov Substitution: any state drops into any car; any strategy drops into the controller
Interface Segregation: one method each: step() and pickCar(); no fat interfaces
Dependency Inversion: the controller depends on SchedulingStrategy, the car on ElevatorState, both injected

blocks.text: Elevator interviews are decided on these. Have an answer ready for each.

metadata.alt: The edge cases the design must survive

items: Request to the current floor: just open the doors; no movement, no state churn
Button spam: the pending set makes repeats free
All cars busy: calls queue in the pending set and dispatch as cars free up; nothing is lost
Obstructed door forever: after K reopens, alarm and take the car out of dispatch
Car pulled mid trip: unserved stops re dispatch; riders inside are delivered to the nearest safe floor first
Top and bottom floors: the sweep reverses naturally because no stop can exist beyond them
Simultaneous UP and DOWN at one floor: two distinct hall keys; possibly two different cars answer

blocks.text: Everything is cheap; the sorted stop set does the heavy lifting.

items: requestPickup: O(M) to score M cars, plus O(log S) to insert into a stop set of size S
requestFloor: O(log S) insertion, with O(1) dedup
step(): O(M) per tick, one state call per car; next stop lookup is O(log S)
getStatus: O(M) snapshot
O(M x S): stop sets across the fleet, bounded by floors, so effectively O(M x N)
O(P): pending hall keys, at most 2N
O(1) extra per request; history lives only in the database journal

blocks.text: The persistent story of an elevator is its trip log, which powers maintenance schedules and traffic tuning.

metadata.alt: Entity relationship diagram for elevator persistence

items: ELEVATOR: one row per car with live floor, status, and lifetime trip count
TRIP: each completed movement with from, to, and timestamps: the analytics gold
REQUEST_LOG: every call with its assigned car, for wait time measurement
MAINTENANCE: service windows per car, feeding availability views
TRIP(car_id, started_at): per car usage and wear reports
REQUEST_LOG(created_at): peak traffic analysis by time of day
MAINTENANCE(car_id, from_ts): current availability lookups

blocks.text: Writes are append only logs, so there is no transactional coupling problem here: the live system is authoritative, the database is its history.
The natural follow ups all push on the scheduler, because that is where elevator engineering actually lives.

items: Cost function scheduling: estimated arrival time instead of raw distance, weighing current stops
Up peak mode: park idle cars at the lobby during morning rush
Zoning: dedicate cars to floor bands in tall buildings to cut travel
Why LOOK over FIFO: FIFO zigzags the car; show 3, 12, 5 served as 3, 5, 12 in one sweep
Where State earns its keep: the overload and door rules live in exactly one state each
Starvation: can a far floor wait forever? The sweep guarantees every stop is passed each cycle
Group control: multiple controllers coordinating banks of cars share the same strategy interface
Telemetry: trips stream to a central service for predictive maintenance
Autonomy: a car must serve its cab calls even if the controller link drops

blocks.text: Walk it in this order and every scored box gets ticked.

items: Open with the split: each car is a State machine, the controller is a Strategy driven scheduler
Draw the car state diagram: Idle, Moving, DoorOpen, and the safety Halted
Explain LOOK with the 3, 12, 5 example: one sweep, sorted order, no zigzag
Show the sorted stop set and why it replaces a FIFO queue
Point at the dedup: two identical presses, one atomic winner
Stress that safety guards live inside states and outrank the scheduler
Contrast strategies: nearest car versus zoned versus up peak, all one interface
Close with starvation: the sweep passes every floor each cycle, so no stop waits forever

blocks.text: Every elevator decision has a defensible alternative; knowing both sides is the senior signal.

FIFO is simpler and fair by arrival, but the car zigzags: 3, 12, 5 travels 9 extra floors. LOOK serves sorted stops per direction and wins on every metric riders feel. Concede FIFO only if the interviewer wants strict arrival fairness.

Central dispatch, as designed, gives globally better assignments and one place to tune. Fully autonomous cars grabbing calls are simpler and survive controller failure. Real systems blend: central assignment, autonomous cab call serving.

We assign a hall call once, at dispatch. Re-evaluating assignments each tick can improve times when traffic shifts, at the cost of complexity and rider confusion when a promised car changes. Immediate assignment is the right interview default; name re-evaluation as the tuning knob.
A step() clock makes the system deterministic and testable, which interviews reward. Real threads per car are closer to hardware but drown the hour in synchronisation noise. Choose ticks and say why.
26.5 State classes versus a status enum
blocks.content: 26.5 State classes versus a status enum

blocks.text: Three modes fit a switch today, but doors, overload, fire service, and maintenance each add arms to every method. State classes keep each mode one small file, and the DoorOpen dwell timer shows why: it is state that belongs to the mode itself.
Real elevator controllers are safety certified embedded systems, and their habits transfer.

items: Safety interlocks in hardware: door and overload circuits physically prevent movement, software mirrors them, never replaces them
Watchdogs: a car that misses heartbeats is pulled from dispatch automatically
Trip journals: every movement logged for maintenance prediction and incident review
Graceful degradation: controller down means cars still serve their cab calls
Monitoring: wait time percentiles, door reopen rates, and per car trip counts on dashboards
Chaos drills: kill a car mid trip in simulation and assert its stops re dispatch
Testing: property tests on the sweep (never passes a pending stop without serving it) and table driven state transition tests
Firmware updates: cars update one at a time, never the whole bank at once

blocks.text: Split the machine from the policy: State drives each car safely, Strategy decides who goes where, and the sweep keeps everyone moving.
